runs.t: Text from social media is full of hashtags, mentions, links, emoticons and stretched-out words, and the tokenizers that most classifiers rely on were not designed with this in mind. In this project we ask whether a lexical analyzer built the way a compiler builds one can do a better job. We built LexFront, a lexer with eleven token classes, longest-match scanning, error recovery, a symbol table and six switchable normalization rules. We also wrote our own engine that turns regular expressions into an NFA, then a DFA, then a minimized DFA. The experiments run on a PLY-based lexer, and our engine is checked against it, because it reproduces the same tokens on four of the token classes. LexFront was compared with whitespace splitting, NLTK and TweetTokenizer, and with BPE, WordPiece and Unigram subword tokenizers, with the classifier kept the same each time. We tested on three core datasets, on a collection of eight cleaned datasets with fair classifier tuning, and on four large datasets: Sentiment140 (1.6 million tweets), Civil Comments and Amazon polarity (about 500,000 training examples each), and Yelp reviews with five star classes (about 300,000 training examples).

The answer is the same everywhere we looked: LexFront is competitive, but it is not better. With the tokenizer as the only change, its accuracy stays close to NLTK and TweetTokenizer on the large datasets, with wide-tuned differences from 0.00 to +0.46 points, and it is clearly ahead only of plain whitespace splitting. It does give the lowest out-of-vocabulary rate and the smallest vocabulary among the word-level tokenizers, and it loses slightly less accuracy when noise is added to the test text. Most of the accuracy we measured comes from the classifier and its tuning, not from the tokenizer: moving from Naive Bayes to Logistic Regression is worth up to 17 points, and wider validated settings add 2 to 3 points for Logistic Regression on Sentiment140, Amazon polarity and Yelp. The subword tokenizers and a character n-gram baseline did not help either. We report these results with confidence intervals and with the hypotheses that did not hold.
Keywords:
lexical analysis, DFA, tokenization, noisy text, text classification, subword tokenization.

A lot of the text we want to classify today comes from social media, and it is messy. People write hashtags, @-mentions, links and emoticons in the middle of sentences, they stretch words out ("soooo good"), and they use slang that no dictionary has. A tokenizer that was built for clean newspaper text can split these things in awkward ways, and since a classifier only sees the tokens, a bad split can cost accuracy. This problem has been known for a while, and early work on tweets already treated tokenization and normalization as problems of their own [2], [3].

Compilers face a very similar problem in their first phase. A lexical analyzer reads a stream of characters and groups them into tokens, using regular expressions, a longest-match rule, a symbol table and some way of recovering from characters it cannot match [1]. That is close to what a tweet tokenizer has to do, so we wanted to see how far the compiler approach carries over. Our idea was to build a lexer in the compiler-design style, use it as a pre-tokenizer for text classification, and compare it with existing tokenizers while keeping everything else in the pipeline fixed. Throughout the paper the existing setup is the NLTK tokenizer with Naive Bayes, and the proposed setup is LexFront with Logistic Regression. The question we try to answer is whether a compiler-style lexer classifies noisy text better than the tokenizers people already use.

The work in this report makes four contributions. First, we built LexFront, a lexer with a priority-ordered token specification, a normalizer and a symbol table, together with our own regex-to-DFA engine that implements Thompson construction, subset construction and Moore minimization. Second, we set up a controlled comparison in which the tokenizer is the only thing that changes, with confidence intervals and significance tests so that small differences are not over-read. Third, we ran ablations that switch each normalization rule off separately, and a subword extension that combines LexFront with BPE and compares it with WordPiece and Unigram [4]. Fourth, we checked how far the results hold up with a fair tuning protocol, a collection of eight cleaned datasets, and four large datasets with hypotheses written down before the runs. Section 2 reviews the literature, Section 3 describes the proposed system and its five parts, Section 4 gives the implementation and results, Section 5 compares performance, and Section 6 concludes.

We grouped the related work into five areas: compiler front ends and automata, tokenization of noisy text, subword tokenization, text classification baselines, and evaluation methodology. Each subsection ends with a short note on how it connects to our work.

blocks.text: 2.1 Compiler front ends and finite automata

runs.t: The standard reference for the first phase of a compiler is the textbook by Aho, Lam, Sethi and Ullman [1], which describes how a lexical analyzer turns regular expressions into a recognizer and how a symbol table and error recovery fit around it. The construction we implement goes back to Thompson [5], who showed how to build a nondeterministic automaton from a regular expression piece by piece. The subset construction that converts it to a deterministic automaton, and the closure properties that make this possible, are covered in the automata theory text by Hopcroft, Motwani and Ullman [6]. For minimization we followed the partition-refinement idea that goes back to Moore [7].

On the practical side, Lex [8] generated scanners from regular expressions and was designed to work together with the parser generator Yacc [9]. PLY [10] brings the same style to Python, and the tokenizer used in our experiments is built on it. All of these tools take a list of patterns in priority order and apply longest match, with ties going to the earlier rule, which is the behaviour we copied. What we take from this area is the whole design vocabulary of LexFront: token classes, longest match, priority, semantic actions on tokens and panic-mode error recovery.

blocks.text: 2.2 Tokenization and normalization of noisy text

runs.t: Gimpel et al. [2] built a part-of-speech tagger specifically for Twitter and had to deal with hashtags, mentions, URLs and emoticons as tokens in their own right, and Owoputi et al. [11] improved it further with word clusters. Han and Baldwin [3] looked at the other side of the problem and studied how to normalize the ill-formed words in short text messages into their standard forms. Later, the shared tasks at the Workshop on Noisy User-generated Text made lexical normalization a regular benchmark [12]. These papers show that for noisy text the choice of what counts as a token, and what is done to it afterwards, is an open design decision and not a solved detail.

Most practical systems use general toolkits. NLTK [13] ships a standard word tokenizer and a TweetTokenizer that handles emoticons, handles and elongation, and these are the two existing tokenizers we compare against. Textbooks on information retrieval also treat tokenization as a step with real consequences for what ends up in the index [14]. Large language models for tweets follow a similar pattern. BERTweet [15], which was pre-trained on English tweets, normalizes user mentions and links before tokenization, which is close in spirit to the placeholders in our normalizer.

Subword methods avoid the unknown-word problem by splitting rare words into smaller pieces. Sennrich et al. [4] adapted byte pair encoding (BPE) for neural machine translation, and the WordPiece model, first described for Japanese and Korean voice search [16], was used in Google's translation system [17]. Kudo [18] proposed a unigram language model for subword segmentation and the SentencePiece toolkit [19] packaged BPE and unigram tokenization in a language-independent way. BERT [20] uses a WordPiece vocabulary and RoBERTa [21] uses byte-level BPE, so these methods sit under most modern language models.

Several papers question whether these tokenizers are optimal. Bostrom and Durrett [22] argue that BPE is suboptimal for language model pretraining and that a unigram-based tokenizer can do better. Rust et al. [23] show that the quality of the tokenizer affects how well multilingual models perform on single languages, and Toraman et al. [24] study how tokenization choices affect language models for Turkish. Mielke et al. [25] give a broad survey of tokenization and open-vocabulary modeling. Bojanowski et al. [26] used character n-gram subwords to enrich word vectors, which is another way of handling rare and misspelled words. Almost all of this work targets neural models trained at large scale. Our setting is smaller and uses a linear classifier, so we do not expect the same conclusions, and we treat the subword results as a separate question.

Multinomial Naive Bayes is a classic text classifier and has been compared closely with other event models by McCallum and Nigam [27]. Wang and Manning [28] showed that simple Naive Bayes-style models with bigrams are strong baselines for sentiment and topic classification, and Joulin et al. [29] made a similar point with fastText, which is a fast linear classifier. Features for such classifiers are usually built with TF-IDF, which combines the idea of inverse document frequency [30] with term weighting schemes studied by Salton and Buckley [31]. Dense representations such as word2vec [32] and GloVe [33], and later the Transformer [34], moved the field toward neural models, but linear models on TF-IDF features remain a common and transparent baseline. We use scikit-learn [35] for TF-IDF, Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression.

We deliberately kept to this baseline setting. A linear model on TF-IDF features is sensitive to exactly the thing we want to study, which is how the text is split into tokens, and it is cheap enough to run the whole grid of tokenizers on full datasets.

Many papers report a difference of a few tenths of a point without saying whether it is bigger than the noise. The bootstrap [36] gives a way to put confidence intervals on a metric by resampling the test set, and McNemar's test [37] compares two classifiers on the same test examples, which is the paired case we have. Dietterich [38] discussed which tests are appropriate for comparing classifiers, and Dror et al. [39] wrote a guide to significance testing for NLP. We follow these ideas: paired bootstrap intervals and McNemar's test for every tokenizer difference, and a note on what the intervals do and do not cover.

From the survey we see plenty of work on tokenizers for neural models and on normalization for tweets, and a long tradition of lexer construction in compilers. What we did not find is a controlled comparison that takes a lexer built with standard compiler machinery and puts it next to existing tokenizers with the classifier held fixed. LexFront and the experiments in this report try to fill that gap on a small scale, and we try to be careful about what the results do and do not show.

The system is a text classification pipeline in which the tokenizer is the part we swap. Raw text goes into one of the tokenizers, the tokens are turned into TF-IDF features, and a classifier (Naive Bayes or Logistic Regression) predicts the label. Because everything after the tokenizer is identical, any difference in the results can be put down to the tokenizer and not to the rest of the pipeline. Around that pipeline we have an evaluation layer that computes accuracy, macro-F1, confidence intervals, significance tests and a few intrinsic measures such as out-of-vocabulary rate and vocabulary size.

We organised the work into five parts. The first is the existing methodology that serves as the baseline. The second is the LexFront lexer and the DFA engine. The third is the normalizer and symbol table together with the ablation of its rules. The fourth is the subword stage, which includes the LexFront + BPE hybrid and the comparison with WordPiece and Unigram. The fifth is the protocol for tuning, scale and robustness: fair classifier tuning, larger datasets, and a noise test. The last four are the new contribution, and we give pseudocode for each of them.

blocks.text: Figure 1. Architecture of the proposed system and its five components

runs.t: The baseline holds the setup that LexFront is compared against. It has three existing tokenizers, which are whitespace splitting, the NLTK word tokenizer and NLTK's TweetTokenizer [13]. Their tokens go into TF-IDF with min_df=2, and the features go into a majority-class baseline, Multinomial Naive Bayes (the existing method) and Logistic Regression with max_iter=1000 and seed 0. Together, the NLTK tokenizer with Naive Bayes is what we call the existing setup. All fits run on a single thread, because we saw that the BLAS thread count changed some Logistic Regression metrics in the last digits. Every run writes a JSON file with its configuration, a fingerprint and the metrics, and stores its test predictions so that the confidence intervals can be computed without refitting.
The evaluation loop shared by all experiments is short, and we give it as Algorithm 1 below.

blocks.title: Evaluation loop shared by all experiments
lines: save record (with config + code fingerprint) and test predictions
tables, figures and statistics are built only from the saved files

runs.t: This is the main new component, and with Logistic Regression behind it, it forms the proposed setup. LexFront defines eleven token classes in priority order (in lexer/token_spec.py): URL, MENTION, HASHTAG, EMOTICON, EMOJI, NUMBER, CONTRACTION, ELONGATED, WORD, PUNCT, and UNKNOWN as the fallback. A PLY-based scanner takes the longest match at each position, ties go to the earlier class, and a character that matches nothing becomes an UNKNOWN token so scanning continues, which is panic-mode recovery.
Our own regex-to-DFA engine and its table-driven scanner are given as Algorithms 2 and 3: Algorithm 2 builds the automaton and Algorithm 3 scans with it.

a.title: Regex to minimized DFA
lines: input : rules [(name_i, regex_i)], in priority order
atoms <- alphabet split at every range boundary
add eps-edge NFA.start -> s ; accepting[t] <- i
if T not empty: add T if new ; trans[S][a] <- T
S.accepts <- min accepting[q], q in S
until the number of blocks stops growing

b.title: Longest-match scanner with error recovery
lines: if text[pos] is whitespace: pos++ ; continue
state <- start ; last <- none ; i <- pos
if last is none:                       # error recovery

runs.t: Besides the PLY lexer we wrote our own engine in
lexer/dfa/

. A recursive-descent parser turns each regular expression into an AST, Thompson construction [5] gives an NFA, subset construction [6] gives a DFA over an alphabet that is split into atoms, and Moore's partition refinement [7] minimizes it. The engine covers four classes (EMOTICON, HASHTAG, MENTION and WORD). The tokenizer used in the experiments is the PLY-based one, and our engine is a separate implementation that a test checks against it: it produces the same tokens on those four classes. ELONGATED is not part of the engine because its usual regex, (.)\1{2,}, needs a back-reference, which regular expressions cannot express.

blocks.text: 3.5 Normalizer, symbol table and rule ablation

runs.t: After a token has been scanned, a semantic action maps it to its canonical form, much like the action block attached to a Lex rule. LexFront has six such rules in
lexer/normalize.py

, and each one can be switched on or off by itself. URLs become <URL>, mentions become <USER> and numbers become <NUM>. Runs of three or more identical letters are shortened to two ("sooooo" becomes "soo"). Word-like tokens are lowercased, and a lookup in a slang table of 30 entries expands things like "u" into "you". The symbol table stores an id, a frequency and a class for each token.

Because every rule has its own switch, we can run an ablation in which one rule is removed at a time, and a case-sensitivity check in which TF-IDF's own lowercasing is turned off. That is how we find out which rules actually help. Pseudocode for the normalizer follows.

blocks.title: Token normalization, tokenization and rule ablation
lines: if cls == URL     and config.url:      return ["<URL>"]
if cls == MENTION and config.mention:  return ["<USER>"]
if cls == NUMBER  and config.number:   return ["<NUM>"]
if cls not in {WORD, CONTRACTION, ELONGATED}: return [lexeme]
lexeme <- shorten every run of 3+ identical letters to 2
if config.slang and lexeme in slang_table:
return split(slang_table[lexeme])          # may be several words
for form in normalize_token(cls, lexeme, config):
ablation: for rule in [url, mention, number, elongated,
run the full pipeline with that rule switched off

blocks.text: 3.6 Subword stage and the LexFront + BPE hybrid

runs.t: The subword stage adds learned vocabularies on top of, and next to, the word-level tokenizers. We trained BPE, WordPiece and Unigram models with the Hugging Face tokenizers library on the training split only, lowercased, with a vocabulary of 8000 pieces (BPE was also run at 32000). Pieces that continue a word carry the ## marker in BPE and WordPiece. We also built a two-stage hybrid that follows the compiler idea of passing different token types to different handlers. LexFront decides the class of each token first. Structural tokens such as placeholders, hashtags, emoticons, emoji, punctuation and error tokens are passed through whole, and only the word-like tokens are handed to a BPE model that was trained on the word-like tokens of the training texts.

Making the training deterministic took some care. The trainer assigns ids to the ## alphabet in hash-map order, so two trainings on the same text could merge in a different order. We fixed this by passing a sorted alphabet as special tokens and removing them from the added-token list afterwards. We also checked that texts from the test split do not leak into the trained vocabularies. The hybrid is described in the pseudocode below.

blocks.title: LexFront + BPE hybrid tokenizer
lines: if cls in {WORD, CONTRACTION, ELONGATED}: words.extend(forms)

runs.t: The last part of the system is about how far the results above can be trusted. It has three parts. The first is a fair tuning protocol. For every tokenizer we choose the TF-IDF settings (word n-grams up to length 3, plain or sublinear term frequency, minimum document frequency 2 or 5) and the classifier parameter (C from 0.3 to 30 for Logistic Regression, alpha from 0.03 to 1 for Naive Bayes) on a validation slice taken from the training data only. The grid is the same for every tokenizer, and the test set is scored once at the end. This matters because a tokenizer comparison at default settings can simply favour whichever tokenizer happens to suit those defaults.

The second part is scale. We cleaned each dataset with fixed rules (empty texts, texts with conflicting labels, duplicates, and test texts that also occur in the training set) and, for Sentiment140, we split by user so that no user appears in both train and test. On Sentiment140 we also ran a size ladder from 10,000 to the full training set. The third part is a noise test: seeded synthetic noise is added to the test text only (a light level, where 10% of the eligible words are corrupted, and a heavy level with 30%), to see which tokenizer loses less accuracy. Hypotheses and a practical margin of plus or minus 0.5 points were written down before the runs in protocol documents (docs/LARGE_PROTOCOL.md, docs/BOOST_PROTOCOL.md and docs/D_PROTOCOL.md). Each difference is then reported as within, beyond or unclear relative to that margin. Algorithm 6 below summarizes the tuning and comparison steps.

blocks.title: Tuning, paired comparison and noise test
lines: fit, val <- stratified split of train (at most 100,000 / 20,000 examples)
for vectorizer in VECTORIZER_GRID:        # word n-grams, raw or sublinear tf, min_df
for value in PARAMETER_GRID[classifier]:      # C or alpha
refit the best setting on the full training set
score the test set once, save predictions
# the same grids are used for every tokenizer
CI   <- percentile bootstrap of diff over the test examples
verdict <- within | beyond | unclear   against the +-0.5 point margin
noise_test(tokenizer): add seeded noise to the test text only; accuracy lost = clean - noisy

runs.t: The system is written in Python and every number below was read from the JSON result files in the repository, which are written by the scripts we ran. The core datasets use full data with no subsampling. For Civil Comments and Amazon polarity we took a seeded random sample of about 500,000 training examples, for Yelp 300,000 training and 50,000 test examples, and Sentiment140 is used in full after cleaning. Each cell is a single training run. The 95% confidence intervals are paired percentile bootstraps over the test examples, with McNemar's test for accuracy on the core datasets. They cover the draw of the test set, not training randomness.

We used English datasets that differ in style and size, in three groups. The core group has three datasets used in the core experiments: tweet_topic [40] has tweets labelled with six topics, go_emotions [41] has Reddit comments labelled with 28 emotion classes (we kept only the single-label examples), and ag_news [42] has news articles in four categories. The first two are noisy and informal, while ag_news is relatively clean, which gives a useful contrast. The collection group adds five tweet_eval tasks (sentiment, emotion, irony, hate and offensive language), so that together with the core datasets there are eight cleaned datasets. The large group has Sentiment140 (1.6 million tweets, split by user), Civil Comments (comments with a toxicity label, where the toxic class is rare), Amazon polarity (product reviews) and Yelp (reviews with five star classes, which tests a many-class problem). Table 1 lists the core and large datasets, and the last column is the share of the largest class in the test set, which is also the accuracy of the majority baseline. For the large datasets the sizes are after cleaning and, for Civil Comments and Amazon polarity, after taking a seeded random sample of about 500,000 training examples (300,000 training and 50,000 test examples for Yelp).

Table 2 gives accuracy and macro-F1 for the three existing tokenizers with each classifier. The first thing we notice is how little the tokenizer matters compared with the classifier. On go_emotions, switching from Naive Bayes to Logistic Regression is worth around 17 points for every tokenizer, while the spread between tokenizers under Logistic Regression is about 2 points. NLTK and TweetTokenizer are slightly ahead of plain whitespace splitting in nearly every row. Naive Bayes on go_emotions is close to the majority baseline in accuracy, and its macro-F1 is very low, which means it mostly predicts the large classes.

Reading Table 2 across the three datasets, the three existing tokenizers stay close together. With Naive Bayes the accuracy is 70.3, 71.0 and 70.8 on tweet_topic for whitespace, NLTK and TweetTokenizer, 37.7, 37.8 and 37.8 on go_emotions, and 90.1, 90.4 and 90.2 on ag_news. With Logistic Regression the same tokenizers reach 70.5, 72.3 and 72.0 on tweet_topic, 53.5, 55.3 and 55.5 on go_emotions, and 91.4, 91.9 and 91.8 on ag_news. Whitespace splitting is the lowest of the three in every Logistic Regression column, by about 2 points on the first two datasets and 0.4 to 0.5 points on ag_news, while changing the classifier moves the accuracy by up to 17 points.

Table 3 shows how big each automaton is. The four classes are small. The combined automaton goes from 43 NFA states to 12 DFA states, and minimization brings it down to 10. WORD shrinks from 3 DFA states to 2 and EMOTICON from 6 to 5, so minimization does remove real redundancy. We also compiled ELONGATED by spelling it out as 26 separate branches, only to see what happens. It is not part of LexFront, but it shows how fast the construction can grow, from 221 NFA states to 157 DFA states and 54 after minimization.

blocks.text: Figure 3. The minimized combined DFA (redrawn from results/module2/dfa_min.dot)

runs.t: Table 4 compares the word-level tokenizers on three intrinsic measures. LexFront has the lowest out-of-vocabulary rate and the smallest vocabulary on all three datasets. On ag_news, for example, its OOV rate is 0.48% against 0.96% for NLTK, and its vocabulary has 65,337 types against 98,994. We need to be careful with this result. Part of it is built in, because placeholders and collapsed letters shrink the vocabulary by design, so it is not evidence of better classification by itself. The accuracy results are the real check, and we look at them next.

blocks.text: Table 4. Intrinsic metrics of the word-level tokenizers (results/module2/intrinsic__*.json)

runs.t: Table 5 gives the main comparison. We call LexFront with Logistic Regression our proposed setup and NLTK with Naive Bayes the existing one. The proposed setup is 17.58 points higher on go_emotions and 1.50 higher on ag_news, and 0.26 lower on tweet_topic, so on the surface it looks good. The last two columns separate the effects. NLTK with Logistic Regression scores about the same as LexFront with Logistic Regression on go_emotions and ag_news, which tells us that nearly all of the gain is the classifier and not the tokenizer. This is why we report the tokenizer-only comparison in Section 5 as the fair one.

blocks.text: Table 5. Proposed (LexFront+LR) versus existing (NLTK+NB), accuracy / macro-F1 (%)

runs.t: Table 6 shows the effect of removing one rule at a time in the main setting, where TF-IDF still lowercases the text. In this setting no single-rule removal gives an accuracy interval that excludes 0, so none of the individual rules shows a clear effect on its own. One more thing explains part of this. The URL rule never fires on tweet_topic and go_emotions, and the mention rule never fires on ag_news, because those datasets already mask URLs and handles. For those cases the removal is not a real test of the rule. The one setting that does stand out is removing every rule on tweet_topic, which raises accuracy by 1.09 points [+0.50, +1.71]. In other words, on that dataset the normalization as a whole does not help.

blocks.text: Table 6. Per-rule ablation, accuracy change versus full LexFront+LR (points, 95% CI), main setting (results/ablation)

runs.t: In the main setting the effect of removing a single rule is small. On tweet_topic the largest changes are +0.50 points for the number rule and +0.41 for the mention rule, on go_emotions the single-rule changes lie between -0.11 and 0.00, and on ag_news between 0.00 and +0.07, and none of these intervals excludes 0. Switching all rules off changes accuracy by +1.09 [+0.50, +1.71] on tweet_topic, by -0.17 [-0.41, +0.07] on go_emotions and by +0.11 [-0.04, +0.25] on ag_news, so only the tweet_topic interval excludes 0, and it points in the direction of the rules not helping.

The case-sensitivity check tells a clearer story. When TF-IDF's own lowercasing is switched off, the lowercase rule inside LexFront becomes the one that matters. Removing it lowers accuracy by 0.91 points on tweet_topic [-1.71, -0.09] and by 1.07 on go_emotions [-1.72, -0.44], while ag_news does not change in a clear way (+0.14 [-0.17, +0.46]). The same check explains a result we noticed earlier. With case kept, LexFront barely moves, with Logistic Regression accuracy changing by only -0.03, -0.02 and +0.04 points on the three datasets, while the baseline tokenizers lose between 0.6 and 1.3 points on tweet_topic and go_emotions, because they leave capitalised words alone. With case kept, LexFront beats NLTK on go_emotions by 1.15 points [+0.46, +1.85]. Our reading is that this advantage comes from the lowercase rule alone, and since TF-IDF lowercases by default, it disappears in the main setting.

blocks.text: Table 7. Case kept (TF-IDF lowercase=False): LexFront+LR minus NLTK+LR, accuracy points [95% CI] (results/sensitivity_case)

runs.t: Table 8 lists the subword runs next to the two word-level references. BPE with a vocabulary of 8,000 shows no accuracy gain over NLTK with Logistic Regression. The intervals include 0 on tweet_topic (-0.41 [-1.27, +0.44]) and go_emotions (-0.04 [-0.68, +0.59]), and on ag_news it is 0.75 points lower [-1.13, -0.37]. The LexFront + BPE hybrid is below LexFront alone on all three datasets, by 0.82, 0.72 and 0.86 points, and 17 of the 24 intervals in the hybrid comparison at vocabulary 8,000 exclude 0, all pointing down. A bigger vocabulary (32,000) reduced this, since 8 of 24 intervals exclude 0 there. Our guess, which we have not tested, is that the hybrid splits up words that the word-level scanner already handled well, so it adds noise. For WordPiece and Unigram, none is above NLTK with Logistic Regression in accuracy with an interval that excludes 0, and on ag_news both are below it (-0.41 and -0.91). The one interval that is above NLTK is Unigram's macro-F1 on go_emotions (+1.26 [+0.10, +2.39]), which is 1 of 30 comparisons and could easily be chance.

blocks.text: Table 8. Subword runs, Logistic Regression, accuracy / macro-F1 (%), vocabulary 8000 (results/bpe, results/subword2)

runs.t: With Logistic Regression and a vocabulary of 8,000, the accuracy on tweet_topic is 72.32 for NLTK and 70.73 for LexFront, against 71.90 for BPE, 71.61 for WordPiece, 73.05 for Unigram and 69.90 for the LexFront + BPE hybrid. On go_emotions the six values lie between 54.64 (hybrid) and 55.71 (Unigram). On ag_news NLTK and LexFront both reach 91.88, while BPE, WordPiece, Unigram and the hybrid reach 91.13, 91.47, 90.97 and 91.03. The intervals given above show which of these differences are more than noise.

The OOV rate of the subword tokenizers is close to zero, for example 0.44% for BPE and 0.31% for WordPiece on tweet_topic, because rare words are split into pieces instead of being left unknown. That number is not comparable with the word-level OOV rates in Table 4, and the price is more tokens per word (fertility goes up to between 1.3 and 1.8).

blocks.text: 4.6 Tuned classifiers on the eight-dataset collection

runs.t: The first question about the earlier results is whether they depend on the default classifier settings. To check, we cleaned eight datasets and tuned the classifier equally for every tokenizer, choosing the TF-IDF setting and C or alpha on a validation slice of the training data. Tuning raised accuracy in 44 of 64 dataset, tokenizer and classifier cells, lowered it in 16 and left 4 equal, with a mean change of +1.63 points. The largest gains are for Naive Bayes, for example +8.12 points on average over the tokenizers on go_emotions and +10.26 on tweet_eval emotion. Table 9 shows what this does to the tokenizer comparison. With default settings, LexFront differs clearly from NLTK on 4 of the 8 datasets (two up and two down). With tuned settings, none of the 8 intervals excludes 0. In other words, tuning removes most of the differences that were visible at default settings, and the test sets of the small datasets are too small to show anything else. The one large positive value, tweet_eval irony, rests on only 784 test examples and its interval just touches 0.

blocks.text: Table 9. LexFront+LR minus NLTK+LR, accuracy points [95% CI] (results/collection/REPORT.md); * = interval excludes 0

runs.t: Sentiment140 has 1.6 million tweets, which is enough to separate small differences from noise. We split by user (5% of users held out, none in both splits), cleaned the data, and ran every tokenizer at default, validation-tuned and wide-tuned settings. The first part of Table 10 is Logistic Regression and the second is Naive Bayes. At default settings the four tokenizers are close, with LexFront at 79.85 against 79.88 for NLTK. With tuned settings every tokenizer gains about 2 to 3 points, and LexFront is highest by a small amount (82.84 against 82.73 for NLTK with the wide setting). The paired differences are small. For Logistic Regression, LexFront minus NLTK is -0.03 [-0.16, +0.10] at default settings, +0.17 [0.00, +0.34] tuned and +0.11 [-0.04, +0.25] wide, all inside the 0.5-point margin. The size ladder shows the same: the mean LexFront minus NLTK gap is +0.12 at 10,000 training examples, +0.10 at 100,000, +0.09 at one million and -0.03 on the full set, so it shrinks toward zero as data grows.

blocks.text: Table 10. Sentiment140 test accuracy (%), word tokenizers and the character n-gram baseline (results/large, results/boost_sentiment140)

runs.t: Two other results from this run are worth reporting. First, in the noise test the tokenizers lose accuracy as expected, and LexFront loses the least (Table 11). With heavy noise, LexFront minus NLTK is +0.14 points, and the difference in accuracy lost is +0.16 [+0.02, +0.32], which is a small effect, well inside the margin, but its interval excludes 0. Second, the character n-gram baseline, which we expected to be a strong competitor for noisy text, is clearly worse here: with wide settings it is 2.74 points below LexFront for Logistic Regression and 5.26 points below for Naive Bayes.

blocks.text: Table 11. Sentiment140, Logistic Regression, default settings, accuracy (%) with added test noise (results/large/REPORT.md)

runs.t: On the practical side, at default settings LexFront produced 104,503 features against 228,086 for NLTK and 226,995 for TweetTokenizer, and tokenized 6,566 test tweets per second, against 4,845 for NLTK, 10,542 for TweetTokenizer and about 1.08 million for whitespace splitting. So it is faster than NLTK and slower than TweetTokenizer on this machine.

blocks.text: 4.8 Wider settings and the character baseline

runs.t: The wide setting in Table 10 is a larger validated grid (word n-grams up to 3, plain or sublinear term frequency, minimum document frequency 2 or 5, and wider C and alpha ranges) that we applied equally to every tokenizer. Compared with default settings, it adds +2.01 points for whitespace, +2.86 for NLTK, +2.57 for TweetTokenizer and +3.00 for LexFront with Logistic Regression, and +3.2 to +3.7 points with Naive Bayes. Compared with the earlier tuned setting the extra gain is small (+0.24 to +0.37 for Logistic Regression). The gain from tuning therefore dwarfs any difference between the word tokenizers. Of the five hypotheses we wrote down for this phase, only one was observed: LexFront stayed within the margin of NLTK and TweetTokenizer. The others were not (Section 5.6).

blocks.text: 4.9 Civil Comments, Amazon polarity and Yelp

runs.t: To see whether Sentiment140 is typical, we ran the same protocol on three more large datasets: Civil Comments and Amazon polarity with about 500,000 training examples each, and Yelp with about 300,000. Civil Comments is a comments dataset where the toxic class is rare (the majority class alone gives 92.02% accuracy), so we use macro-F1 as the primary metric there. Amazon polarity is clean review text and acts as a control. Table 12 gives the wide-tuned results. On Civil Comments, LexFront, NLTK and TweetTokenizer are essentially tied, and all three are clearly ahead of whitespace splitting in macro-F1: LexFront minus whitespace is +2.25 points [+1.79, +2.70] for Logistic Regression, and with default settings +4.03. On Amazon, LexFront and TweetTokenizer are level with each other (-0.01 [-0.09, +0.07]) and both are ahead of NLTK, with LexFront minus NLTK at +0.46 [+0.34, +0.57]. That interval is above zero but crosses the 0.5-point margin, so we label it unclear and not a clear gain. Wider settings help a lot here: +2.8 to +3.3 points for Logistic Regression and +5.7 to +6.7 for Naive Bayes on Amazon.

Yelp has five star classes (balanced, so the majority class gives 20.00%), which makes it the one many-class large test. The result is again the same. With wide settings and Logistic Regression, LexFront minus NLTK is +0.07 points [-0.16, +0.31] and LexFront minus TweetTokenizer is -0.15 [-0.37, +0.07], both inside the margin, while LexFront is +1.08 [+0.76, +1.38] ahead of whitespace splitting, which is beyond the margin. With Naive Bayes, LexFront minus NLTK is -0.09 [-0.28, +0.11]. Wide settings add +2.63 to +3.15 points for Logistic Regression and +5.4 to +6.3 for Naive Bayes compared with default settings, again much more than any difference between the word tokenizers.

blocks.text: Table 12. Wide-tuned test results, accuracy / macro-F1 (%) (results/boost_civil_comments, results/boost_amazon_polarity, results/boost_yelp_full)

runs.t: A caution on how these three runs were made. They ran on a Windows laptop with Python 3.12, while the Sentiment140 runs ran on Colab. Each run records its own library versions, so the results are valid but should not be mixed at the digit level. The Yelp run needed about 10 hours of fitting time in total, and an earlier attempt on Colab did not finish.

This section pulls the comparison together. We use two metrics, accuracy and macro-F1. Macro-F1 matters on tweet_topic and go_emotions, where the classes are unbalanced, because a model can have decent accuracy by favouring the large classes. We also report paired 95% bootstrap intervals and McNemar's test, so that each difference comes with a statement of how large the test-set noise is.

blocks.text: Figure 6. Existing (NLTK+NB) versus proposed (LexFront+LR), accuracy and macro-F1

runs.t: Figure 6 shows the headline comparison, which is the same one as in Table 5. The proposed setup is higher on go_emotions and ag_news and about level on tweet_topic in accuracy. In macro-F1 it is higher on all three, by 7.62 points on tweet_topic and 29.09 on go_emotions. The tokenizer-only comparison in Table 13 shows where that comes from.

blocks.text: 5.2 Separating the tokenizer from the classifier
Table 13. Paired differences, accuracy points [95% CI] (results/stats/bootstrap.json)

runs.t: Reading Table 13 row by row, the tokenizer-only differences are the fair test of LexFront. On go_emotions and ag_news the intervals include 0, so LexFront and NLTK are indistinguishable there. On tweet_topic LexFront is 1.59 points lower and that difference is significant (McNemar p < 0.001). The proposed-minus-existing rows are large on go_emotions and ag_news, but almost all of that is the move from Naive Bayes to Logistic Regression: with NLTK held fixed, the classifier change alone is worth +17.49 on go_emotions and +1.50 on ag_news. So we do not claim that LexFront is better. What the data support is that it does about as well as NLTK on two of the datasets and somewhat worse on one, and that it gives a smaller vocabulary and a lower OOV rate.

blocks.text: Figure 7. LexFront+LR minus NLTK+LR, accuracy points with 95% intervals; the green band is the plus or minus 0.5 point practical margin

runs.t: Figure 7 puts the tokenizer-only comparison for Logistic Regression on all twelve datasets in one place. The tuned or wide-tuned setting is used, so that the comparison is not tied to default settings. The picture is clear. Ten of the twelve point estimates lie inside the margin. The two exceptions are tweet_eval hate (-0.66) and irony (+3.06), and both have wide intervals that include values inside the margin. The four large datasets have much narrower intervals, and they are tight around zero: +0.11 on Sentiment140, 0.00 on Civil Comments, +0.46 on Amazon polarity and +0.07 on Yelp. The small datasets have wide intervals, because their test sets are small, so they cannot rule out a difference of a point or more in either direction. The only point far from zero, tweet_eval irony, has the widest interval and rests on 784 test examples. There is no dataset where LexFront is clearly better than NLTK by more than the margin, and none where it is clearly worse once the classifier is tuned. We read this as "competitive", not "better".

On the intrinsic side, LexFront has the lowest OOV rate and the smallest vocabulary among the word-level tokenizers on the three core datasets, with fertility close to the others. On Sentiment140 it also gives the smallest feature set. Part of this is built in, because placeholders and collapsed letters shrink the vocabulary by design, so it is a description and not evidence of better classification. Speed is in the same range as the other tokenizers. On the core datasets it runs at about 0.84 to 1.48 times the speed of NLTK, and on Sentiment140 at 6,566 tweets per second against 4,845 for NLTK. The lexer is therefore not a bottleneck. The subword tokenizers (Table 8) are not clearly better than NLTK in accuracy on the core datasets, and the character n-gram baseline is clearly worse on Sentiment140.

Looking at the three core datasets in turn, the OOV rate for whitespace, NLTK, TweetTokenizer and LexFront is 18.5%, 8.7%, 9.9% and 8.2% on tweet_topic, 6.0%, 2.6%, 2.6% and 2.4% on go_emotions, and 1.9%, 1.0%, 0.8% and 0.5% on ag_news. Fertility is 1.00 for whitespace by definition and between 1.15 and 1.43 for the other three. The vocabulary of LexFront has 14.5 thousand entries on tweet_topic, 24.5 thousand on go_emotions and 65.3 thousand on ag_news, against 21.7, 44.5 and 158.7 thousand for whitespace splitting, 15.7, 26.4 and 99.0 thousand for NLTK, and 16.5, 25.9 and 86.1 thousand for TweetTokenizer.

Table 14 compares the size of the different changes we tried. The pattern is consistent across datasets. The classifier and its tuning move accuracy by several points, and the tokenizer moves it by a fraction of a point once the classifier is tuned. This is the main finding of the project, and it is more useful than a single headline number.

runs.t: Because we wrote hypotheses and a decision rule before each large run, we can say which ones held. Table 15 lists them. Several of our own expectations were not supported, and we report them as such. For example, we expected wider tuning to push every tokenizer beyond the earlier tuned setting (HA1), and it did not, and we expected the character n-gram baseline to be at least as good as LexFront (HA4), and it was clearly worse.

runs.t: A few cautions apply to all of the numbers. There is one training run per cell, so training randomness is not covered by the intervals, which only measure test-set sampling. We ran many comparisons and did not correct for multiple testing. In the rule ablation, 6 of 42 interval comparisons exclude 0 when about 2 would be expected by chance. All datasets are English, and all large ones except Yelp are two-class, so we cannot say anything about other languages or code-mixed text, and Yelp is our only many-class test at scale. We did not test transformer models. The Colab and laptop runs used different library versions, which each run records. All reasons we give for why a difference appears are hypotheses, not tested conclusions.

We built LexFront, a compiler-style lexer for noisy English text, with our own regex-to-DFA engine, a normalizer with six switchable rules, a symbol table and error recovery, and compared it with existing and subword tokenizers under a fixed classifier. The engine works as intended: the combined automaton goes from 43 NFA states to 12 DFA states and 10 minimized states, and it agrees with the PLY lexer on the four classes it covers. The classification experiments themselves run on the PLY-based lexer.

On the question we started with, the answer is that a compiler-style lexer is competitive but not better. This held on the three core datasets, on the eight-dataset collection with fair tuning, and on four large datasets with about 300,000 to 1.5 million training examples, one of them with five classes. With the tokenizer as the only change, LexFront stays within about half a point of NLTK and TweetTokenizer on the large datasets, and its clear advantage is over plain whitespace splitting, especially in macro-F1 on Civil Comments and by about one point on Yelp. It gives a smaller vocabulary, a lower out-of-vocabulary rate and slightly smaller accuracy losses under added noise. Most of the accuracy comes from the classifier and its tuning. BPE, WordPiece, Unigram and the character n-gram baseline did not improve on the word-level tokenizers, and several of our own hypotheses were not supported, which we report as they came out.

The main limits are one training run per cell, English-only data, and no transformer baseline. Natural next steps are repeating the large runs with other random seeds, running the character baseline on the two newer datasets, testing across domains (training on one source and testing on another), and trying a tweet-trained transformer model, which would use its own tokenizer and therefore test a different question.
